sun.title: Why does the Sun's elevation matter?
sun.body: With no atmosphere, there is no twilight on the Moon: either direct sunlight arrives or it does not. The higher the Sun, the more energy horizontal panels receive. At the south pole the Sun skims the horizon, so a distant mountain or a crater rim can leave a site in darkness.

earth.title: Why does seeing Earth matter?
earth.body: To talk to Earth without relay satellites, the antenna has to 'see' Earth above the horizon. From the Moon, Earth barely moves in the sky, but it wobbles a little (libration). Near the edge of the near side, that wobble makes Earth appear and disappear.

horizon.title: Geometric horizon and real horizon
horizon.body: The geometric horizon assumes a smooth, round Moon. The real horizon is set by mountains and craters: at the south pole (85°–90° S) we use the terrain measured by the LOLA altimeter, and there a few kilometres can change the hours of light a lot. Elsewhere, for now, the geometric horizon is used.
